sections.html:
You will find the recorder at 209 S. Blackhoof St., Suite 103, Wapakoneta, Ohio 45895. Weekday hours run from eight in the morning to half past four. The phone is 419-739-6735 and the fax is 419-739-6736.

Down the hall, so to speak, is the treasurer at the same street address, 419-739-6745. One trip can cover both a deed filing and a tax payoff.

Whatever passes title to land here, or puts a burden on it, lands in the recorder's permanent files. The earliest property records date to 1848, when Auglaize County was formed, and the books are preserved in archival form for public use.

  • More than 1,000 sections of the Ohio Revised Code touch the recorder's duties.
  • A seat on the records commission, which sets retention periods for county records, belongs to the recorder.
  • The office runs the county microfilming department.
  • Fees collected at the counter go into the county general fund.
  • Every year the office prompts commissioners and township trustees to file their zoning resolutions, maps and amendments.

A fee schedule is posted on the recorder's page, and it is the place to find the amount to send with a deed.

Statewide fees come from ORC 317.32, and the local schedule operates inside that law.

Recording fees under ORC 317.32
ServiceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Recording and indexing, first two pages$17$17
Each subsequent page$4$4
Marginal reference by separate instrument$2$2
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Local fax or electronic transmission, per page$1$1

Counties can tack on a preservation charge of up to $5, credited to the general fund. Ask whether Auglaize County does.

sections.h2: Deed transfer fee and the auditor
sections.html:
Transfer fees are not the recorder's business. They go to the auditor, whose office is separate. That office also keeps the records of deed transfers, homestead exemptions, oil and gas wells, special assessments and all real property, exempt parcels included. A statement of value comes first, which ORC 319.202 requires from the buyer.

Under ORC 319.54(G)(3) the fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, whichever is higher, and the seller pays. The commissioners can add a Chapter 322 transfer tax as well, so find out from the auditor whether it applies. Three kinds of transfer are exempt: those that only give or release security for a debt, those ordered by a court that are not themselves sales, and those that correct a deed already on record.

sections.h2: How values are set and challenged
sections.html:
Valuation is the auditor's job as chief assessor, with a reappraisal every six years and an update every three. A Board of Revision, the auditor, the treasurer and one commissioner, hears testimony on complaints.

The deadline in ORC 5715.19(A)(1) is whichever comes later, March 31 after the tax year or the close of first-half collection. Mail is dated by Postal Service postmark rather than a private meter. If unpaid land tax could be on your parcel, ask the treasurer before listing.

In 2020 the county had 19,873 housing units, 6.4% vacant, and owners lived in 75.6% of occupied homes. Wapakoneta is the largest community and has the courthouse. Because owners dominate, most sales are plain house-to-house deeds. Selling a parent's house or leaving the state does not change the recording steps, and as-is sales work the same.

sections.h2: Treasurer and auditor duties in a sale
sections.html:
Voters elect the treasurer for four years, and the office serves as the county's banker. The office collects real property and personal taxes, plus taxes on manufactured homes, hotel-motel stays and special assessments, and holds the money collected for schools, cities, townships and villages until it is distributed. The staff is small, two full-time employees, so call ahead for a payoff figure instead of showing up on closing day.

The auditor does the assessing. Beyond reappraisals, the auditor registers manufactured homes and assesses their value, then passes the proceeds to municipalities, townships and school districts in proportion. The auditor also sits with the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney on the budget commission, which oversees the tax rates other subdivisions set.

  • Payoff and delinquent balances: treasurer, 419-739-6745.
  • Statement of value, homestead and parcel records: auditor.
  • Deed and mortgage recording: recorder, 419-739-6735.

sections.h2: Typical documents and who files them
sections.html:
A normal house sale generates a deed and, when the seller has a loan, a release of the mortgage. If the seller has died, an affidavit or court papers may also be needed to show who can sign. Each document is its own recording, and the page count drives the fee in the table above. Title companies bundle these filings and send them in together, which is why many sellers never meet the recorder in person.

If you are selling on your own, the practical risk is a rejected packet. A missing auditor endorsement, a legal description that differs from the last deed, or a wrong payment amount will send you back to start. One call to the recorder before you leave prevents all three problems.

sections.h2: Why recording matters to a seller
sections.html: Recording is what puts the sale on the public record, and the recorder's index is where the next buyer's title search will find it. A deed that is signed but never recorded leaves the record showing the old owner, which leaves the buyer without a clean record of ownership. Ask the closing agent for confirmation that the deed was filed.

• Recorder, 419-739-6735, with a fax line at 419-739-6736.
  • Treasurer, 419-739-6745, for tax payoffs and delinquent balances.
  • Auditor, for the statement of value, homestead records and the transfer fee.

Call the recorder to confirm the fee total, the treasurer for a payoff before the closing date, and the auditor before you carry the deed over. Taking the calls in that order keeps the paperwork moving in the order the county needs it, and it saves a second drive to Wapakoneta. People selling a house they inherited or one they are leaving from out of state can do most of this by phone and mail, as long as the auditor's endorsement is already on the deed.

sections.h2: What to bring to record a deed
sections.html:
Take the signed, acknowledged deed, the auditor-endorsed value statement and payment matching the county schedule. Mailing it? Phone 419-739-6735 first and confirm the total. Hold on to the last recorded deed so you can match the legal description.

Save the recorded deed and value statement with your closing papers. A title company running the closing usually sends the deed in for you, after which the index lists the new owner.

One workable order: obtain a payoff from the treasurer, prepare the deed, visit the auditor for the endorsement, then record. A cash purchase drops the lender's paperwork but not these visits or fees.

faqs.q: What are the Auglaize County Recorder's hours?
faqs.a: Eight to half past four, Monday through Friday, at 209 S. Blackhoof St., Suite 103, Wapakoneta. The phone is 419-739-6735.

faqs.q: How far back do Auglaize County property records go?
faqs.a: To 1848. The books are kept permanently in archival form.

faqs.q: What fees does Auglaize County add for a deed?
faqs.a: State law sets $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for pages one and two, then $4 plus $4 per added page. The posted county schedule shows local totals.

faqs.q: Which office collects the conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The auditor does. Sellers pay $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, if higher, and any Chapter 322 county tax.

faqs.q: Where do I contest my property value?
faqs.a: File with the auditor, for the Board of Revision, by March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.
